title: The River That Ran Short
sources: Every claim is checked against episodes/colorado-river/research.md (sources, own calculations, both sides of contested points).
Decision: Interior press release 21 Aug 2026 [R1]; Greenberg Traurig [R3]; cuts AZ 760,000 (-27.1 %), CA 440,000 (-10 %), NV 50,000; Minute 334 signed 2 Sep 2026, Mexico -250,000 a year [R7].

Levels and storage: Reclamation daily CSVs (Powell 919, Mead 921) via tools/colorado_numbers.py: Powell 3,516.62 ft on 15 Sep 2026, Mead 1,037.16 ft on 22 Oct 2026; combined 46.45 MAF (1 Jan 2000) -> 11.95 MAF (16 Sep 2026); Powell area -63 %; WY 2026 release 6.0 MAF; ten years WY 2017-2026 = 80.0 MAF.

Snow and inflow: Interior (lowest observed snowpack on record); Reclamation October 2026 24-Month Study (April-July 18 % of average; August about 0; evaporation Mead 457,000 + Powell 181,000 AF; Mead lows 1,007.73 ft (6 maf run) and 1,015.68 ft (7 maf run)).
Compact: text [R19]; 16.4 MAF assumption, 14.76 (1906-2018), 12.47 (2000-2018) [R20]; 75 vs 82.5 MAF readings and Kuhn's 'first tripwire' [R16].

Dam: Reclamation memo 2024 [R14] (1,320 MW, 3,490 ft minimum power pool, four river outlet works, cavitation, not envisioned to run solely on them); 710 ft (Reclamation Quick Facts); dead pool 3,370 ft; USGS SIR 2022-5017 [R12].

Own map: tools/powell_shoreline.py (USGS 2017 multibeam bathymetry): 225.1 / 188.5 / 77.7 km2 at the record low / 3,490 / 3,370 ft, within 2 % of the USGS 2018 EAC table; 1.34 MAF between the record low and 3,490 ft.

Use: Richter et al. 2024 (74 % of direct human use, three times all other direct uses, cattle feed 46 %); SNWA via The Nevada Independent (198,000 AF in 2025, -40 % in 25 years, +800,000 people); NPS (Las Vegas 90 % from Lake Mead); SNWA (intakes 1,050 / 1,000 ft, Intake No. 3 2015, pumping station 2020).

Lawsuit: Nevada 24 Aug 2026 [R3][R4]; Arizona DWR and CAP 16 Oct 2026, Burgum quote [R6]; Lombardo quote [R4]; Hobbs 'draconian' [R6]; Upper Basin governors 9 Apr 2026 (coyotegulch); CPR 9 Sep 2026 [R16].
October storm: ABC15 [R11] (65,000 cfs, second-highest October daily inflow since 1963); Reclamation data (Powell +16.84 ft from 15 Sep to 2 Nov).

paragraphs.text: This is Lake Powell, on the border of Utah and Arizona, in the summer of 2019. It is the second largest reservoir in the United States. Now watch the same bays in September 2026.

On September 15th, Lake Powell fell to its lowest level since it first filled. Five weeks later, Lake Mead, behind Hoover Dam, set a record low of its own. Together the two lakes held less water than at any time since 1963. The river they store supplies more than forty million people, from Denver to Los Angeles, and about five million acres of farmland.

After three years of talks, the seven states that share the river could not agree on new rules, so on August 21st the federal government wrote them itself. Arizona, California and Nevada must use 1.25 million acre-feet less water a year in 2027 and 2028. The four states upstream face no required cuts. Three days later, Nevada sued.

document.text: Consensus on long-term operations did not materialize.

shots.on_screen_text: 1.25 million acre-feet a year less, in 2027 and 2028

paragraphs.text: So when a river runs short, who should give up water first? The answer goes back to a deal struck in 1922, for a river that turned out to be smaller than its negotiators believed.

shots.photo: Colorado River Compact. Signed at Santa Fe, New Mexico, November 24, 1922 - DPLA - 5f58da61d22c5517da996253ca29cdf2 (page 1).jpg

shots.at: for a river that turned out
shots.subtitle: Seven states, two lakes and a promise from 1922

paragraphs.text: The Colorado starts as snowmelt high in the Rocky Mountains and runs south-west through deep canyons to the Gulf of California. Its basin reaches into seven American states and into Mexico.

In November 1922, delegates from the seven states met in Santa Fe and split the river in two at Lee Ferry, a crossing in northern Arizona. Colorado, Utah, Wyoming and New Mexico became the Upper Basin. Arizona, California and Nevada became the Lower Basin. Each half got the right to use seven and a half million acre-feet a year. One acre-foot is about 326,000 gallons, enough to flood a football field a foot deep.

stat.label: acre-feet a year for each basin

paragraphs.text: The upper states also promised not to let the flow at Lee Ferry fall below 75 million acre-feet over any ten years. In 1944, a treaty added one and a half million acre-feet a year for Mexico. Keep that ten-year number in mind, because the states are now fighting over it.

shots.photo: Lees Ferry Colorado River 1870, C.R. Savage.jpg

stat.label: acre-feet past Lee Ferry in any ten years
stat.note: the upper states' promise, Article III(d)

shots.on_screen_text: 1944 treaty: 1.5 million acre-feet a year for Mexico

shots.query: Colorado River flowing through red rock canyon

paragraphs.text: The negotiators counted on about 16.4 million acre-feet a year, based on the short gauge record they had, and those early years were wet. Over the full record since 1906, the river has averaged about 14.8 million. From 2000 to 2018 it averaged about 12.5 million. The deal divided more water than the river carries.

shots.photo: Colorado River Compact. Signed at Santa Fe, New Mexico, November 24, 1922 - DPLA - 5f58da61d22c5517da996253ca29cdf2 (page 13).jpg

shots.at: based on the short gauge record

chart.title: River flow, million acre-feet a year
chart.source: Reclamation natural flow data, via Kuhn and Fleck

paragraphs.text: For decades, two giant reservoirs covered the gap. Hoover Dam was finished in 1936 and filled Lake Mead. Glen Canyon Dam began storing water in 1963, and Lake Powell first filled in 1980. At their peak in July 1983, the two lakes held 52.5 million acre-feet, about three and a half years of the river's average flow.

shots.photo: GRCA 33720 1958 Hidden Passage Canyon in Glen Canyon Mile 76.jpg

shots.on_screen_text: July 1983: 52.5 million acre-feet in the two lakes

shots.at: about three and a half years

stat.label: of the river's average flow, held in the two lakes
stat.note: 52.5 million acre-feet at the peak, July 1983

paragraphs.text: Lake Powell drowned Glen Canyon, a maze of side canyons, photographed here in the 1950s. Today more than four million people a year visit the lake.

shots.photo: GRCA 117031 1954 Tapestry Wall in Glen Canyon Mile 136.2.jpg

paragraphs.text: Those two lakes are only half of the system. The other half carries the river hundreds of miles from its banks, to cities that grew up far away from it.

shots.photo: ALL-AMERICAN CANAL CARRIES COLORADO RIVER WATER THROUGH SAND-SWEPT AREA OF THE IMPERIAL VALLEY - NARA - 549076.jpg

paragraphs.text: Follow the water past Hoover Dam to Lake Havasu, on the Arizona-California line. There, two pumping plants lift it out of the river. One sends it west through the Colorado River Aqueduct, about 240 miles to the Los Angeles area. The other sends it east through the Central Arizona Project, 336 miles of canal, pumped nearly three thousand feet uphill to Phoenix and Tucson.

Farther south, at Imperial Dam, the All-American Canal turns it west, about 80 miles to the Imperial Valley in California, desert that the canal turned into farmland. What is left of the river crosses into Mexico, where Morelos Dam diverts most of it to farms and cities there.

shots.photo: IRRIGATED FIELDS OF THE IMPERIAL VALLEY, NEAR EL CENTRO - NARA - 548813.jpg
shots.where_label: Imperial Valley near El Centro, California, 1972

paragraphs.text: So who uses all this water? A 2024 study led by Brian Richter added up every use from 2000 to 2019. Irrigated farming takes 74 percent of the water people use directly, three times as much as all the cities, homes and industries combined. Hay and alfalfa grown to feed cattle take 46 percent on their own.

document.text: New water accounting reveals why the Colorado River no longer reaches the sea
document.source: Richter et al., Communications Earth & Environment, 2024

chart.title: Who uses the river's water
chart.source: Richter et al. 2024, direct human use 2000-2019 (CC BY 4.0)

paragraphs.text: Cities have been cutting back. Las Vegas gets about 90 percent of its water from Lake Mead. Southern Nevada now uses about 40 percent less river water than it did 25 years ago, while adding more than 800,000 people. In 2025 it used 198,000 acre-feet, about two thirds of its share.

stat.label: Colorado River water used by Southern Nevada than 25 years ago

paragraphs.text: Farms hold many of the oldest water rights on the river. Cities hold most of the people. When there is not enough for both, which should give way first? Is hay grown in the desert a waste of the river, or exactly what those old rights were meant to protect? I want to know where you stand.

ask.text: Desert hay: a waste of the river, or what old rights protect?

shots.query: hay bales in a field aerial

shots.at: or exactly what those old rights

paragraphs.text: Lake Mead's history fits in one line. It began filling in 1935 and rose and fell with wet and dry years for decades. In 1983 it never dropped below 1,200 feet. Since 2000 it has mostly gone down. In 2021 the government declared the first official shortage on the river. In July 2022 the lake hit a record low just above 1,040 feet, and this October it went lower, to 1,037.

chart.title: Lake Mead, lowest level each year

shots.query: Lake Mead low water level drought

shots.at: and this October it went lower

stat.label: Lake Mead's record low, October 22, 2026
stat.note: the old record: 1,040.6 ft in July 2022

paragraphs.text: Lake Powell followed the same path. We added up the Bureau of Reclamation's daily records for both lakes. In January 2000 they held 46.5 million acre-feet together. On September 16th this year they held 12 million. About three quarters of the water was gone.

chart.title: Lake Powell, lowest level each year
Water in Powell and Mead, million acre-feet
chart.source: Bureau of Reclamation daily data; our calculation

stat.label: of the water in Lake Powell and Lake Mead gone since January 2000
stat.note: 46.5 million acre-feet then, 12.0 million on September 16, 2026
stat.source: Bureau of Reclamation daily data; our calculation

paragraphs.text: From orbit, the change is plain. This is Lake Powell in September 2000, seen by NASA's Terra satellite, and here it is in September 2026. By Reclamation's measurements, its surface has shrunk by almost two thirds.

stat.label: Lake Powell's surface, September 2026 against January 2000
stat.source: Bureau of Reclamation area data; our calculation

paragraphs.text: Then came the winter of 2025 to 2026, with the smallest snowpack ever recorded in the basin. Here are Colorado's mountains in March 2023, a big snow year, and in March 2026. From April through July, when the snowmelt should pour in, the runoff headed for Lake Powell was 18 percent of average. In August, apart from water let out of reservoirs upstream, almost nothing flowed in.

Lake Powell had been this low once before. In April 2023 it set what was then a record, and a snowy winter lifted it almost 65 feet by July. Three years later it was lower than ever. The white band on the canyon walls marks where the water used to stand.

stat.label: Lake Powell's rise from April to July 2023

paragraphs.text: On Lake Mead's northern arm, coves that held water in the spring of 2020 are now dry land. But the number engineers fear most is upstream, at Glen Canyon Dam. In September, Lake Powell was just 27 feet above it.

shots.at: In September, Lake Powell was just

stat.label: between Lake Powell and the turbine line, September 2026

paragraphs.text: Glen Canyon Dam is 710 feet tall, and its power plant can generate 1,320 megawatts. If the lake falls below 3,490 feet above sea level, the turbines can no longer run. That line is called the minimum power pool.

stat.label: minimum power pool: below it, Glen Canyon Dam's turbines stop

paragraphs.text: Below that line, the only way to move water downstream is through four smaller tunnels called the river outlet works. The Bureau of Reclamation says the dam was never meant to run on those tunnels alone for long, and it is studying how to limit cavitation damage inside them. At 3,370 feet, water cannot leave through the dam at all. Engineers call that dead pool.

document.highlight: Establishment of Interim Operating Guidance for Glen Canyon Dam during Low Reservoir Levels at Lake Powell
document.title: Technical Decision Memorandum, 26 March 2024

shots.where_label: Glen Canyon Dam's river outlet works, 2018

stat.label: dead pool: below it, no water can leave Glen Canyon Dam

paragraphs.text: We wanted to see those lines on the map. In 2017 the U.S. Geological Survey mapped the bottom of Lake Powell with sonar, and we used that survey to find where the water would stand. This is the lake at its record low in September. At 3,490 feet it would look almost the same from space, about 16 percent smaller. At dead pool, about two thirds of it would be gone, and the lake would end just below Bullfrog Bay.

document.highlight: Beginning in 2017, the U.S. Geological Survey, in cooperation with the Bureau of Reclamation, completed topobathymetric surveys of Lake Powell
document.title: Scientific Investigations Report 2022-5017

shots.on_screen_text: Our map · from the USGS sonar survey of the lakebed

paragraphs.text: At the record low, about 1.3 million acre-feet stood between the lake and the turbine line, less than three months of this year's releases. To protect that line, the government had already cut the 2026 release from Glen Canyon Dam to 6 million acre-feet, the smallest in sixty years. It also ordered up to a million acre-feet sent down from Flaming Gorge Reservoir, on the Wyoming-Utah line.

stat.label: acre-feet between Lake Powell and the turbine line

chart.title: Released from Glen Canyon Dam, million acre-feet
chart.source: Bureau of Reclamation daily data (water years); our calculation

shots.on_screen_text: Up to 1 million acre-feet from Flaming Gorge

paragraphs.text: Downstream, Las Vegas prepared years ago. Its first intake in Lake Mead stopped working when the lake fell below 1,050 feet. A second works down to 1,000. A third, finished in 2015, with a pumping station added in 2020, can keep drawing water even below Hoover Dam's dead pool. Reclamation's October forecasts show Lake Mead falling to between about 1,008 and 1,016 feet by next summer.

shots.on_screen_text: Intake 3 and its pumps: below Hoover's dead pool

paragraphs.text: Hoover Dam has its own lines. Its turbines stop at 950 feet, and at 895 feet no water can pass the dam. Reclamation already lowers its estimate of Hoover's generating capacity as the lake drops.

stat.label: Hoover Dam's turbines stop below this level
stat.note: at 895 ft no water can pass the dam

shots.photo: Generators Inside Hoover Dam, The Tour (3467682551).jpg

paragraphs.text: We check stories like this one from orbit, with real satellite images and survey data. If you want to see where Lake Powell's shoreline stands after next spring's snowmelt, subscribe.

The rules that have run the river since 2007 expire at the end of 2026. Talks between the seven states on what comes next began years ago and missed one deadline after another. On July 31st the Interior Department published its final environmental study, and on August 21st it signed the decision.

shots.query: Lake Powell aerial red rock water

paragraphs.text: For 2027 and 2028 the cuts fall on the Lower Basin. Arizona loses 760,000 acre-feet a year, 27 percent of its share. California loses 440,000, ten percent. Nevada loses 50,000. Under a new agreement signed in September, Mexico gives up 250,000 acre-feet a year. The four upper states have voluntary conservation goals and no required cuts.

Arizona takes the biggest cut because of a deal it made in 1968. To get Congress to build the Central Arizona Project, the state accepted a junior priority, so in a shortage the canal's water is cut before California's. In 2026 the canal was expected to divert about 943,000 acre-feet. Tom Buschatzke, who runs Arizona's Department of Water Resources, says cities and farms along the river with the same priority will share some of the cut.

stat.label: acre-feet the Central Arizona Project was to divert in 2026

shots.at: cities and farms along the river

paragraphs.text: We compared the cuts with Reclamation's own numbers. In 2026, Lake Mead and Lake Powell lost 638,000 acre-feet to evaporation alone. That is 84 percent of Arizona's cut, and more than twice Nevada's entire share of the river.

Why are the upper states left out? Washington runs the two big reservoirs, but water rights upstream are run by the states. And there is the ten-year number from 1922. The upper states read the Compact as a promise not to let the flow at Lee Ferry fall below 75 million acre-feet in ten years. The Lower Basin says the real line is 82.5 million, because the upper states also owe half of Mexico's water. We added up Reclamation's release records. In the ten years through September 2026, 80 million acre-feet passed Glen Canyon Dam, below the Lower Basin's line and above the Upper Basin's. Eric Kuhn, a former Colorado water manager, calls it the Compact's first tripwire.

shots.photo: Colorado River Compact. Signed at Santa Fe, New Mexico, November 24, 1922 - DPLA - 5f58da61d22c5517da996253ca29cdf2 (page 11).jpg

chart.title: The ten-year line at Lee Ferry, million acre-feet
chart.source: Colorado River Compact; Kuhn and Fleck

shots.at: because the upper states also owe

chart.title: Ten years past the dam, million acre-feet
chart.source: Bureau of Reclamation daily data; our calculation

paragraphs.text: Both sides have a case. In April, the four upper governors said their states are already enforcing mandatory, uncompensated cuts on water rights that go back to the 1800s, and their states are sending stored water down from Flaming Gorge. Nevada's governor, Joe Lombardo, says Southern Nevada could lose more than 70 percent of its allocation after 2028. Arizona's governor, Katie Hobbs, calls the cuts draconian.

document.text: Mandatory, uncompensated, and will have significant impacts on water users.
Southern Nevada could lose more than 70 percent of its already meager Colorado River allocation.

document.source: Gov. Katie Hobbs, Arizona, on the cuts

paragraphs.text: So should the four upper states share the cuts, even if the Compact may not require it? Or is a deal from 1922 still a deal? Tell me which side you are on.

ask.text: Should the four upper states share the cuts?

shots.query: snowy Rocky Mountains river valley Colorado

shots.photo: Colorado River Compact. Signed at Santa Fe, New Mexico, November 24, 1922 - DPLA - 5f58da61d22c5517da996253ca29cdf2 (page 13).jpg

paragraphs.text: Nevada did not wait. On August 24th, the state, its Colorado River Commission and the Southern Nevada Water Authority sued the Interior Department in federal court in Nevada. They say Interior broke federal environmental and administrative law and misread the Law of the River, and they want the decision thrown out. Nevada also argues that Interior never studied what deep cuts would do to Southern Nevada's $180 billion economy.

shots.query: Las Vegas strip at night aerial

stat.label: Southern Nevada's economy, which Nevada says Interior never studied
stat.source: Nevada's lawsuit, via The Nevada Independent

paragraphs.text: On October 16th, Arizona's Department of Water Resources asked to join the case, and the Central Arizona Project filed its own request. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum says the lawsuit will be thrown out, because, as he put it, you can't be injured in theory. Interior's formal answer to Nevada's complaint was due at the end of October.

shots.at: and the Central Arizona Project filed

shots.on_screen_text: Doug Burgum, Secretary of the Interior

document.text: You can't be injured in theory.
document.source: Doug Burgum, Secretary of the Interior

paragraphs.text: Behind the lawsuit is a bigger threat. If the ten-year flow keeps falling, the Lower Basin could take the Compact itself to the Supreme Court, which hears disputes between states. Experts told Colorado Public Radio that such a case could take years, and that everybody loses.

chart.title: Ten years past the dam, million acre-feet
chart.source: Bureau of Reclamation daily data; our calculation

document.source: Experts on a Supreme Court Compact case, via Colorado Public Radio

paragraphs.text: Should judges decide how this river is shared, or should the states be forced back to the table until they agree? What would you do?

ask.text: Judges, or the states back at the table?

shots.at: or should the states be forced

paragraphs.text: Then, in late October, it rained. Storms over northern Arizona and southern Utah sent 65,000 cubic feet of water per second into Lake Powell, the second highest October flow since 1963. By November 2nd the lake had risen almost 17 feet from its record low.

shots.query: storm clouds rain over desert canyon

stat.label: flowing into Lake Powell in the late-October storms
stat.note: the second highest October flow since 1963

paragraphs.text: The storms helped. Reclamation's October forecasts, made just before them, still had Lake Mead heading for a new low next summer. A wet winter would buy time, but it would not make the river carry what was promised in 1922.

shots.photo: Colorado River Compact. Signed at Santa Fe, New Mexico, November 24, 1922 - DPLA - 5f58da61d22c5517da996253ca29cdf2 (page 1).jpg

paragraphs.text: Even the upper states call this a stopgap. In July their four governors wrote that the basin is seeing the lowest reservoir levels in its history, and that the new framework does not represent a final solution. It runs until 2036, and after 2028 it allows cuts in the Lower Basin of up to 3.6 million acre-feet a year.

document.text: Today's framework does not represent a final solution.
document.highlight: does not represent a final solution

chart.title: Lower Basin cuts, acre-feet a year

paragraphs.text: At the end of the line, the river that carved the Grand Canyon now rarely reaches the sea. Under the new agreement, the United States and Mexico keep a joint program to look after the habitat that is left in the delta. So who should give up water first: the farms, the cities, or the states upstream? Tell me what you think.

ask.text: Who should give up water first?

youtube.title: Lake Mead and Lake Powell Both Hit Record Lows in 2026
youtube.description:
In September 2026 Lake Powell fell to its lowest level since it filled, and in October Lake Mead followed. After three years of failed talks, Washington wrote the river's new rules itself: Arizona, California and Nevada lose 1.25 million acre-feet a year, the four states upstream face no required cuts, and Nevada sued. We mapped Lake Powell at the line where Glen Canyon Dam's turbines stop and at dead pool from the USGS sonar survey of the lakebed, and checked the 1922 Compact's ten-year test against Reclamation's own records.

Real Copernicus Sentinel-2 and NASA MODIS images, USGS and Bureau of Reclamation data, and our own calculations.
youtube.pinned_comment: Who should give up water first when the Colorado runs short: the farms with the oldest rights, the cities with the most people, or the four states upstream? The 1922 Compact may now be headed for court. Where do you stand?
